# Buffer Management and Memory Layout {#sec-buffer-management}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

The previous chapter introduced the `TupleBuffer` as the unit of
inter-operator data flow. This chapter is about where those buffers
come from, where they go, and how they are laid out in memory.

The story is short. NebulaStream uses a pool: a pre-allocated array
of fixed-size buffers, recycled with reference counting. Memory
layout is a property of each buffer, decided once during
optimisation. There is no virtual memory subsystem, no swapping, no
buffer-pool replacement policy more sophisticated than "give me a
buffer, I'll give it back."

The design is austere. The reasons it works are interesting.

---

## 4.1 The pool: pre-allocated, fixed-size, recycled {#sec-pool}

The buffer manager lives in `nes-memory/include/Runtime/BufferManager.hpp`.
The defaults reveal the design:

```cpp
// nes-memory/include/Runtime/BufferManager.hpp
class BufferManager final
    : public std::enable_shared_from_this<BufferManager>,
      public BufferRecycler,
      public AbstractBufferProvider {
    static constexpr auto DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE = 8 * 1024;
    static constexpr auto DEFAULT_NUMBER_OF_BUFFERS = 1024;
    static constexpr auto DEFAULT_ALIGNMENT = 64;
public:
    static std::shared_ptr<BufferManager> create(
        uint32_t bufferSize = DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE,
        uint32_t numOfBuffers = DEFAULT_NUMBER_OF_BUFFERS,
        const std::shared_ptr<std::pmr::memory_resource>& memoryResource
            = std::make_shared<NesDefaultMemoryAllocator>(),
        uint32_t withAlignment = DEFAULT_ALIGNMENT);
};
```

The default configuration: 1024 buffers of 8 KiB each, 64-byte
aligned. That is 8 MiB of buffer memory, allocated up front, on
worker startup, and not released until shutdown. Buffers are
returned to the pool when their reference count drops to zero, not
freed individually.

Three things in this design deserve a closer look.

**Pre-allocation.** Allocating 8 MiB on startup costs one `mmap` and
one zero-fill. Once the engine is warm, no buffer-related allocation
occurs on the hot path. This eliminates a class of latency spikes
that show up in interpreted-language engines, where garbage collection
or first-touch faulting can add milliseconds to an otherwise fast
operation. NebulaStream pays the entire memory bill at startup and
gets predictable steady-state behaviour in exchange.

**Fixed buffer size.** Every buffer is 8 KiB. There is no buffer
class hierarchy with small buffers and big buffers. Variable-size
data — strings, blobs — that does not fit alongside fixed-width
columns goes into a *child buffer*, also from the pool, also 8 KiB,
linked into the parent's lifetime. This means a few common cases
waste memory: a `VARSIZED` field of 100 bytes still takes a full 8
KiB child. The trade-off is operational simplicity: the pool has
exactly one slot size, the recycler has exactly one path, and the
allocator never has to consult a free-list of differently-sized
chunks.

**64-byte alignment.** Modern x86_64 CPU lines are 64 bytes. Aligning
the buffers to a cache-line boundary makes the JIT's vectorised
code much happier; misaligned loads/stores are not free, even on
hardware that "supports" them. ARM is similar.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 4.1: a buffer's life"}
A worker thread needs a buffer to write the output of a projection.
It calls `bufferManager.getBufferBlocking()`, which:

1. Pops a buffer pointer from the pool's `folly::MPMCQueue`.
2. Increments the buffer's reference count from 0 to 1.
3. Resets the metadata (origin, sequence, etc.) to defaults.
4. Returns a `TupleBuffer` wrapper to the caller.

The worker fills the buffer, attaches it to a `WorkTask`, and
sends it onwards. Three operators downstream, the last consumer
of the buffer goes out of scope. The `TupleBuffer` destructor
fires, decrements the count to 0, and returns the buffer pointer
to the pool's queue. No `delete`, no `free`, no `mmap`.
:::

---

## 4.2 What happens when the pool is empty {#sec-pool-empty}

The pool can be exhausted. With 1024 buffers and a query graph of
ten operators each holding two buffers in flight, you can support
about 50 concurrent worker threads before pressure starts. In
practice, the engine sizes the pool to the workload; the default of
1024 is a starting point, not a target.

When the pool is empty, `getBufferBlocking` does what its name
says: it blocks. A worker thread waiting for a buffer is, in effect,
backpressured. This is the engine's third backpressure mechanism, in
addition to the source-side admission queue (Chapter 15) and the
slow-sink-throttles-source pattern that emerges from the worker
thread pool. All three feed into the same end-to-end behaviour: a
slow consumer slows down a fast producer.

The non-blocking variant `getUnpooledBuffer` exists for
emergencies — it allocates a fresh buffer outside the pool — but
its use is rare and discouraged. The intent is that the pool is the
only path.

---

## 4.3 Memory layout: row vs. columnar {#sec-memory-layout}

A schema and a buffer size do not determine where the bytes go. A
buffer of 1024 tuples each consisting of two `UINT64` fields could
be laid out as:

- **Row layout.** `[(field1, field2), (field1, field2), …]`. All
  fields of a tuple together; tuples adjacent.
- **Column layout.** `[field1×1024, field2×1024]`. All values of one
  field together; fields separate.

Column layouts are usually faster for scans that touch a subset of
fields (the famous OLAP advantage). Row layouts are usually faster
for operations that touch every field of a tuple at once (the OLTP
advantage). Streaming workloads land between: aggregations love
columnar; per-tuple projections that touch most fields prefer row.

NebulaStream's optimiser has a phase called `DecideMemoryLayoutRule`,
in `nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Static/DecideMemoryLayoutRule.hpp`.
The phase is small:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Static/DecideMemoryLayoutRule.hpp
// For now, we use row-layout across all operators.
class DecideMemoryLayoutRule {
public:
    LogicalPlan apply(LogicalPlan plan) const;
};
```

The current implementation picks row layout for every plan. The
phase exists, the infrastructure for columnar layouts is in place,
the JIT-level support for both layouts is there — but the optimiser
unconditionally chooses row.

::: {.callout-warning title="Caveat: columnar is a future direction"}
The decision to default to row layout is documented in the
optimiser as deliberate. Columnar support is partly implemented in
`nes-nautilus/` (the Record interface supports both), and a future
optimiser pass will make a per-operator choice. As of the pinned
commit, however, "memory layout" is a single decision applied
uniformly. Treat the framework as ready for an upgrade rather than
the upgrade itself.
:::

---

## 4.4 The MemoryProvider abstraction {#sec-memory-provider}

A buffer + a layout + a schema is enough information to read and
write tuples. NebulaStream wraps these in a `MemoryProvider`
interface that the JIT code uses to access fields. The
`MemoryProvider` knows the layout and produces, for each field
access, the correct pointer arithmetic. It is the indirection that
makes "row vs. columnar" a per-buffer choice rather than a global
choice.

In code-generated terms: when the JIT lowers a `Record::read("value")`,
it asks the `MemoryProvider` for the address calculation. For a row
layout, the address is `base + tupleIndex * tupleSize +
fieldOffset`. For a columnar layout, it is `base + fieldOffset *
numTuples + tupleIndex * fieldWidth`. Both layouts produce code
that is nearly as fast as a hand-written loop.

We will see the JIT side of this in Chapter 12.

---

## 4.5 The pmr escape hatch {#sec-pmr}

The `BufferManager::create` signature takes a
`std::pmr::memory_resource`. By default it is
`NesDefaultMemoryAllocator`, which calls into the system allocator.
The escape hatch is there because workloads on specialised hardware
(GPUs, ARM accelerators, persistent-memory devices) may want to
allocate buffers from an arena that is not main memory. Plumbing
that arena through the standard `pmr` interface keeps the rest of
the engine unchanged.

This is one of the seams where NebulaStream's "heterogeneous
hardware" vision shows up in code: a future GPU backend would
provide a `pmr::memory_resource` that allocates from device
memory, and the buffer manager would be unchanged.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch4-summary}

NebulaStream's buffer manager is a pre-allocated pool of fixed-size
(default 8 KiB), 64-byte-aligned, reference-counted buffers
distributed via a folly MPMC queue. The design is austere — no
size classes, no variable allocations on the hot path, no swap —
because the simplification pays for the underlying assumption that
the workload fits in main memory. Memory layout (row vs. columnar)
is decided per-buffer by an optimiser phase that currently hardcodes
row, with the columnar support stubbed in for future work. The
`pmr::memory_resource` extension point allows future hardware
backends to provide alternative allocators without touching the
rest of the engine.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch4-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 4.1: pool exhaustion"}
Reduce `DEFAULT_NUMBER_OF_BUFFERS` from 1024 to 8 in a local copy
of `BufferManager.hpp` and rebuild. Run a join systest:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1
```

Does the test still pass? How does throughput change? Where does
the engine spend time when buffers are scarce?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 4.2: confirm the layout"}
Insert an `NES_DEBUG` log inside `DecideMemoryLayoutRule::apply`
that prints the layout chosen for each operator. Run any systest
in INTERPRETER mode. Confirm — for now — that every operator gets
row layout.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 4.3: variable-size payloads"}
Run a systest that uses `VARSIZED` fields, e.g.,
`nes-systests/operator/join/JoinWithVarSized.test`. Trace one
buffer through the engine. How are child buffers attached? When
does a parent's destructor release a child?
:::
